topics.title: Composition vs Inheritance
topics.summary: React favors building components by combining them (props, children, slots) rather than extending classes.
topics.description:
In classical OOP, you might reuse code by creating `class SpecialButton extends Button`. React's recommendation is the opposite: **use composition**. Facebook has thousands of components and found no case that required component inheritance.

### Composition tools

1. **Containment** - a generic component renders `props.children`: `Card`, `Modal`, `Layout`.
2. **Specialization** - a "specific" component renders a "generic" one with preset props: `<DangerButton>` renders `<Button variant="danger" />`.
3. **Slots** - pass JSX through named props: `<Layout sidebar={<Nav />} content={<Feed />} />`.
4. **Custom hooks** - share logic (not UI).
5. **Context** - share data without drilling.

### Why composition wins

- **Explicit data flow:** you see which props go in.
- **Flexible:** change markup at the call site without editing the library component.
- **No fragile base-class problem:** changing a base class cannot silently break children.
- **Easy to test.**

### Anti-pattern: boolean prop explosion

`<Button primary large rounded outline icon loading />` grows endlessly. Prefer variants (`variant="primary"`) or composition (`<Button><Icon/> Save</Button>`).

### Sharing non-UI logic

If you want to reuse a function, import it. If you want to reuse stateful logic, write a custom hook. Neither needs inheritance.
keyPoints: Use props, children and slots to reuse UI
Specialize by rendering a generic component with preset props
Custom hooks share logic; plain modules share functions
Avoid boolean prop explosion; use variants
Inheritance between components is almost never needed
pitfalls: Creating deep class hierarchies of components.
Adding a new boolean prop for every design tweak.

examples.title: Specialization with slots
examples.css: .dialog { border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 8px; padding: 10px 14px; margin-bottom: 10px; max-width: 280px; }

interview.q: Why does React prefer composition over inheritance?
interview.a: Composition via props, children and slots is explicit and flexible, while inheritance couples components and has not been needed in large React codebases.

interview.q: How do you share logic between components without inheritance?
interview.a: Extract it to a custom hook (stateful logic) or a plain utility function.

topics.title: Render Props
topics.summary: A component takes a function prop (or children as a function) and calls it to decide what to render.
topics.description:
A **render prop** is a prop whose value is a function that returns JSX. The component owns some logic or state and lets the caller decide how to display it. ```jsx

{x}, {y}

} /> // or, children as a function {({ x, y }) =>

{x}, {y}

} ``` ### How it works `MouseTracker` keeps state for the position and, inside its own render, returns `props.render(position)`. The caller supplies the markup. This separates **what data** from **how it looks**. ### Why it existed Before hooks, render props (and HOCs) were the main way to share stateful logic. Libraries such as React Router (``), Downshift, Formik (``), and React Spring used them. ### Today Most logic-sharing cases are now handled by **custom hooks**, which are simpler and avoid nesting ("wrapper hell"). Render props are still useful when: - The shared component also **renders DOM** (virtual list, tooltip, autocomplete) and the caller must customize each item: `renderItem={(item) => ...}`. - You need to pass data into a **subtree** that a hook cannot reach. - A library API wants flexible output. ### Tips - The render function runs every render; avoid expensive work inside. - If the render prop creates inline functions, memoized children might still re-render.
keyPoints: Function prop that returns JSX
children can also be a function ("function as child")
Separates logic/data from presentation
Mostly replaced by custom hooks for pure logic
Still great for renderItem-style customization
pitfalls: Callback hell: deeply nested render props are hard to read.
Expecting memo to help when the render prop is an inline function.

examples.title: List with renderItem

interview.q: What is the render props pattern?
interview.a: Passing a function prop that a component calls to know what to render, so the component supplies logic and the caller supplies UI.

interview.q: Why are custom hooks preferred over render props now?
interview.a: Hooks share logic without extra nesting or wrapper components and read like normal code.

topics.title: Higher-Order Components (HOC)
topics.summary: A HOC is a function that takes a component and returns a new, enhanced component.
keyPoints: HOC = function(Component) -> Component
Do not mutate; pass through props
Never create a HOC inside render
Set displayName for debugging
Hooks replaced most HOC use cases
pitfalls: Calling withX(Component) inside a component body, which remounts every render.
Losing refs or static properties on the wrapped component.

examples.title: withHoverHighlight HOC

interview.q: What is a higher-order component?
interview.a: A function that takes a component and returns a new component with extra props or behavior, without modifying the original.

interview.q: Why must HOCs not be created inside render?
interview.a: Each render would create a new component type, so React would unmount and remount the subtree and lose its state.

topics.title: Compound Components
topics.summary: A set of components that work together and share implicit state, like select and option.
topics.description:
HTML has natural compound elements: `<select>` and `<option>`, `<table>` with `<tr>` and `<td>`. In React, a **compound component** pattern gives you the same expressive, flexible API for your own widgets: Tabs, Accordion, Menu, Dropdown.

```jsx
<Tabs defaultValue="a">
  <Tabs.List>
    <Tabs.Tab value="a">One</Tabs.Tab>
    <Tabs.Tab value="b">Two</Tabs.Tab>
  </Tabs.List>
  <Tabs.Panel value="a">First</Tabs.Panel>
  <Tabs.Panel value="b">Second</Tabs.Panel>
</Tabs>
```

### How it is built

The parent (`Tabs`) holds the state and shares it with its sub-components through **Context**. Children read state from context, so the user does not pass props manually and the layout can be reordered or wrapped freely.

### Benefits

- **Flexible markup** - the consumer controls structure and order.
- **Clean API** - fewer props, no config arrays.
- **Encapsulated state** - the internal logic is hidden.
- Used by Radix UI, Headless UI, Reach UI, Chakra, MUI.

### Implementation tips

- Use `createContext` and a custom hook that throws when used outside the parent.
- Attach children as static properties: `Tabs.Tab = Tab`.
- Make accessibility part of the pattern: ARIA roles and keyboard handling.
- Support controlled mode (`value` + `onValueChange`) and uncontrolled (`defaultValue`).
keyPoints: Parent shares state with children through Context
Consumer arranges the sub-components freely
Attach parts as Tabs.Tab / Tabs.Panel
Throw if a sub-component is used outside its parent
Used by Radix UI, Headless UI and design systems
pitfalls: Using React.Children.map + cloneElement, which breaks when wrapped.
Skipping ARIA roles and keyboard support in widgets.

examples.title: Tabs as compound components

interview.q: What is the compound components pattern?
interview.a: A group of components that share implicit state via Context so the consumer can compose them flexibly, like Tabs, Tabs.List, Tabs.Tab and Tabs.Panel.

interview.q: Why use Context rather than cloneElement for compound components?
interview.a: Context works even when children are wrapped in other elements or fragments, whereas cloneElement only reaches direct children.

topics.title: Controlled vs Uncontrolled Components
topics.summary: Controlled components get their value from props/state; uncontrolled ones keep it internally in the DOM or their own state.
topics.description:
This concept applies to inputs **and** to any reusable component with a value (toggle, tabs, accordion, modal open state).

### Controlled

The parent owns the state and passes `value` plus `onChange`. The component is a pure view of props.

- Single source of truth in React.
- Easy validation, formatting, syncing and resetting.
- More code and re-renders.

### Uncontrolled

The component (or the DOM) holds its own state. You set an initial value with `defaultValue` / `defaultOpen` and read the result with a ref, `FormData`, or an `onChange` notification.

- Less code, fewer renders.
- Harder to reset or validate live.

### Supporting both in your own component

Good library components (Radix, MUI) accept both: if the `value` prop is given they are controlled, otherwise they manage internal state.

```jsx
function useControllable(value, defaultValue, onChange) {
  const [inner, setInner] = useState(defaultValue);
  const controlled = value !== undefined;
  const current = controlled ? value : inner;
  const set = (v) => { if (!controlled) setInner(v); onChange?.(v); };
  return [current, set];
}
```

### Choosing

Use **uncontrolled** with `FormData` for simple submit-only forms. Use **controlled** when the UI reacts to the value while typing or when other components depend on it.

### Never mix

Switching between the two for the same element (value going from `undefined` to a string) triggers a warning and bugs.
keyPoints: Controlled: value + onChange from the parent
Uncontrolled: defaultValue and internal state
Library components often support both modes
FormData is great for simple uncontrolled forms
Do not switch modes during the lifetime of a component
pitfalls: Passing value={undefined} initially and a string later.
Making every input controlled when the value is only needed on submit.

examples.title: Same widget in both modes

interview.q: Controlled vs uncontrolled components?
interview.a: Controlled components get their value and change handler from the parent state; uncontrolled components manage their own state internally and are read via refs or callbacks.

interview.q: Can a component support both modes?
interview.a: Yes. If the value prop is defined it is controlled; otherwise it uses internal state initialized from defaultValue.

topics.title: Container and Presentational Components
topics.summary: Separate components that know how things look from components that know how data is loaded and managed.
topics.description:
A classic way to organize components:

- **Presentational components** care about *how things look*. They receive data and callbacks via props, rarely have state (only UI state), and are easy to reuse and test (or document in Storybook).
- **Container components** care about *how things work*: fetching, state, calling APIs, connecting to Redux. They render presentational components and pass data down.

### Example

`UserList` (presentational) renders `users` it is given. `UserListContainer` fetches the users and passes them in.

### Modern take

Dan Abramov, who popularized the idea, later said you do not have to follow it strictly. **Hooks** let you separate logic without separate container components: put the logic in a custom hook (`useUsers`) and call it in the same component or a thin parent. The *principle* remains useful: keep rendering code free of data-fetching details.

### Benefits

- **Reusability** - the same view with different data sources.
- **Testing** - test the view with plain props, mock the hook separately.
- **Design system friendly** - dumb components can live in a UI library.
- **Cleaner components** - less mixing of concerns.

### Guidelines

- Presentational components should not import API clients or stores.
- Pass data as props; pass actions as callbacks.
- Do not split just for the sake of it; a tiny component that fetches and renders is fine.
keyPoints: Presentational: how it looks (props in, JSX out)
Container: how it works (data, state, side effects)
Custom hooks can replace container components
Easier reuse, testing and Storybook stories
Do not over-split small components
pitfalls: Mixing API calls and heavy markup in one huge component.
Making presentational components import global stores.

examples.title: Presentational list + container hook

interview.q: Container vs presentational components?
interview.a: Containers handle data and logic; presentational components just render props. This separation improves reuse and testing.

interview.q: How have hooks changed this pattern?
interview.a: Logic can be extracted into custom hooks, so you often don't need separate container components.

topics.title: Portals
topics.summary: createPortal renders children into a different DOM node while keeping them in the same React tree.
topics.description:
Sometimes a component must visually escape its parent: modals, tooltips, dropdowns, toasts. If the parent has `overflow: hidden`, `transform` or a low `z-index`, a child cannot overlay everything. **Portals** render children into another DOM node, typically `document.body`. ```jsx import { createPortal } from "react-dom"; function Modal({ children }) { return createPortal(
{children}
, document.body); } ``` ### Key behaviors - **Events bubble through the React tree**, not the DOM tree. A click inside a portal still bubbles to React parents (useful, but surprising). - **Context works** through portals - they are still children of the provider. - State and lifecycle are the same as any child. - Only the physical DOM location changes. ### Typical use: accessible modal 1. Render into `document.body` via portal. 2. Add `role="dialog"` and `aria-modal="true"`. 3. Move focus into the dialog and **trap focus**; restore focus on close. 4. Close on **Escape** and overlay click. 5. Lock body scroll. The native `` element with `showModal()` also solves much of this, and is rendered in the top layer without a portal. ### Notes In a runnable preview, `document.body` is fine. In SSR, wait until mounted before using `document`.
keyPoints: createPortal(children, domNode)
Same React tree, different DOM location
Events bubble through React parents; context still works
Use for modals, tooltips, toasts, dropdowns
Remember focus trap, Escape key and aria attributes
pitfalls: Forgetting stacking contexts and z-index even with portals.
Using document.body during server rendering.

examples.title: Modal via portal
examples.css:
.overlay { position: fixed; inset: 0; background: rgba(0,0,0,.45); display: grid; place-items: center; font-family: sans-serif; }
.dialog { background: #fff; padding: 16px 20px; border-radius: 10px; min-width: 240px; }

interview.q: What is a portal in React?
interview.a: A way to render children into a DOM node outside the parent's DOM hierarchy while keeping them in the same React tree.

interview.q: Do events bubble from a portal to its React parent?
interview.a: Yes. Events bubble according to the React component tree, not the DOM tree.

topics.title: Error Boundaries
topics.summary: Catch rendering errors in a subtree and show a fallback UI instead of a blank screen.
topics.description:
If a component throws an error while rendering, React unmounts the **entire tree** by default, leaving a white screen. An **error boundary** catches errors from its children and renders a fallback.

### What they catch

- Errors during **rendering**
- Errors in **lifecycle methods**
- Errors in **constructors** of children

### What they do NOT catch

- Errors in **event handlers** (use try/catch)
- **Async** code (setTimeout, promises, fetch)
- **Server-side rendering** errors
- Errors thrown in the boundary itself

### Class component required

There is still no hook for it. A boundary uses `static getDerivedStateFromError(error)` to switch to a fallback and `componentDidCatch(error, info)` to log. Most teams use the **`react-error-boundary`** library, which gives `ErrorBoundary`, `fallbackRender`, `resetKeys` and `useErrorBoundary` (to forward async errors).

### Where to place them

- One around the whole app (last resort).
- Around risky or independent widgets (charts, comments) so a failure does not take the page down.
- Around each route.

### Recovery

Offer a "Try again" button that resets the boundary state, or use `resetKeys` so it resets when props change.

### Logging

Send errors and component stacks to Sentry or similar from `componentDidCatch`.
keyPoints: Catches render/lifecycle errors in descendants
Does not catch event handler, async or SSR errors
Must be a class (or use react-error-boundary)
Place at app, route and widget level
Provide reset and report errors to a logging service
pitfalls: Expecting an error boundary to catch errors thrown inside onClick.
One boundary at the root only, so a tiny widget crash hides everything.

examples.title: Class error boundary with retry

interview.q: What errors do error boundaries not catch?
interview.a: Errors in event handlers, asynchronous code, server-side rendering and errors thrown by the boundary itself.

interview.q: How do you implement an error boundary?
interview.a: With a class component defining getDerivedStateFromError and/or componentDidCatch, or with the react-error-boundary library.

topics.title: Suspense and React.lazy: Code Splitting
topics.summary: lazy loads a component only when needed, and Suspense shows a fallback while it loads.
topics.description:
By default, a bundler puts your whole app in one JavaScript file. **Code splitting** breaks it into chunks that load on demand, making the first page load faster. ### React.lazy ```jsx const Settings = lazy(() => import("./Settings")); ``` `lazy` takes a function that returns a dynamic `import()` promise resolving to a module with a **default export**. The component is downloaded the first time it renders. ### Suspense `}>` shows the fallback while any child below it is "suspended" (waiting for a lazy component, or data from a Suspense-enabled source). ```jsx Loading...

}> ``` ### Where to split - **Routes** (most common): each page is a chunk. - **Heavy, rarely-used UI**: charts, rich text editors, modals, admin panels. - **Libraries** used on a single screen. ### Tips - Place Suspense boundaries thoughtfully; several smaller ones give a better UX than one global spinner. - Combine with an **error boundary** to handle chunk loading failures (offline, new deploy). - Preload on hover or intent: call the import function early. - Use `startTransition` when switching to avoid hiding already-visible UI. - Named exports need an adapter: `.then(m => ({ default: m.Chart }))`.
keyPoints: lazy(() => import(...)) defers loading a component
Suspense shows a fallback while loading
Split by routes and heavy features
Wrap with error boundary for failed chunks
lazy expects a default export
pitfalls: Lazy-loading tiny components, adding more requests than it saves.
No Suspense ancestor, causing an error when a lazy component renders.

examples.title: Lazy component with simulated delay
examples.explanation: The import is simulated with a promise; in a real app use import().

interview.q: What does React.lazy do?
interview.a: It defers loading a component's code until it is first rendered, using a dynamic import, enabling code splitting.

interview.q: Why wrap lazy components in Suspense?
interview.a: Suspense provides the fallback UI shown while the component's code is loading; without it React throws.

Replace multiple booleans with a status value
useReducer is a lightweight state machine

examples.title: Fetch state machine with reducer

interview.q: Why model UI as a state machine?
interview.a: It makes impossible states unrepresentable, clarifies transitions, and makes behaviour easier to test and reason about.

interview.q: How can useReducer act as a state machine?
interview.a: Switch first on the current status and then on the event type, so each state only handles events that are valid for it.
